paras: The assault on Ike Johnson was a roadside attack on a Black man and his wife by two armed white men near the northern edge of Austin, Texas, on the night of January 2, 1882. When Officer J. L. Watts tried to arrest the two men at a house of ill fame later that night, one of them, Emmet McPhail, was shot dead and the other, Jeff Ake, wounded Watts. Papers outside Austin reported the episode as the killing of an ex-convict, and the attack on Johnson was described in detail mainly in the Austin Statesman's inquest coverage.

Ake, whom the Statesman called "a somewhat notorious" character, had been pardoned in May 1881 while serving a penitentiary sentence for the theft of a gelding. McPhail, a stranger in Austin of about nineteen or twenty, had worked for Ake, and the Statesman reported that both men had been drinking.

In the Statesman's first account, Johnson was driving home from church with his wife when two white riders came up on either side, whipped his horses and, when he remonstrated, drew six-shooters and threatened to kill him. Johnson's sworn testimony at the inquest was fuller: after he gave the two men the road near Bertram's old store at about eleven o'clock and warned Ake, "Look out, mister, this may cost you something," they wheeled back and pointed pistols at him and his wife. They made the couple repeat "didn't we like it" several times, Ake lashed Johnson's horse with a buggy whip, and the other man gave his name as "Garfield" before both galloped off.

Johnson found Watts and described the men and their horses, and the two traced them to Sallie Daggett's house in the First Ward. When Watts told the men they were under arrest, both drew pistols; Watts knocked McPhail off the steps and grappled with Ake, who fired and struck him in the side. At Watts's call, William J. McLellan, who was unarmed, took the officer's pistol and shot McPhail, who by McLellan's account was advancing with his pistol aimed at Watts. Ake was overpowered and jailed.

Justice Wilson Gregg's inquest jury found that McLellan fired the fatal shot "in pursuance of duty" while assisting a peace officer, a verdict the Austin special called justifiable homicide. Interviewed in jail, Ake denied attacking Johnson, saying he had been mistaken for someone else, and said he fired at Watts in self-defense without knowing he was an officer.

In mid-January Ake was released on bonds totaling $1,100 on charges of assault with intent to kill, theft of a gelding, and carrying a six-shooter. The report did not say whom the assault charge concerned, and no charge for the attack on Johnson is named in the coverage. In March Ake's bond was recorded as forfeited and his case continued; no report of a trial was found.

The Statesman ran the story under headlines such as "Sad End" and "An Unknown White Man Killed in a Bagino," treating the killing at the brothel as the main event and the attack on Johnson as its cause. It printed the inquest testimony in full, including Johnson's statement signed with his mark, and followed Ake's case through a jail interview, the text of his pardon and his release on bond. Its reporter called Johnson "a colored man," while the jail interview called him "the negro man" and recorded Ake's denial without comment.

An Austin special printed on January 4 by the Dallas Daily Herald and the Waco Daily Examiner mentioned the assault in a single clause, and the Waco paper headed it "A Pardoned Ex-Convict Killed by an Officer." A Galveston relay in the Savannah Morning News on January 5, headed "An Ex-Horse Thief Killed," left the assault out entirely.

The reporter's version had the riders whip Johnson's horses and threaten to kill him after he protested, while Johnson testified to a quarrel over the road, pistols pointed at both him and his wife, and a whip laid on his horse. Ake denied any part in the attack, but Johnson identified him under oath and Watts testified that he had a full description of the men before finding them.

bases: Two white men drew pistols on Johnson and his wife, threatened to kill him and whipped his horse, with no beating, shooting at or injury of the couple (A3, A4).
The Statesman reporter (A3), Johnson's and Watts's sworn testimony (A4) and the Austin special (A1) agree on the assault, but Ake denied taking part in it (A6).

accounts.gist: Johnson, returning from church with his wife, was overtaken by two white riders who whipped his horses and, when he protested, drew six-shooters and threatened to kill him.

accounts.label: Ike Johnson's sworn testimony
accounts.gist: After he gave the road and warned Ake, the men wheeled back, pointed pistols at him and his wife, forced them to repeat 'didn't we like it', and Ake lashed his horse; they later intercepted him downtown.

accounts.label: Jeff Ake (jail interview)
accounts.gist: Denied attacking Johnson, saying he was mistaken for someone else; said he and McPhail were out 'upon a lark' and he fired once in self-defense, not knowing Watts was an officer.

accounts.label: Austin special telegram
accounts.gist: Ake and McPhail had 'assaulted a colored man' returning from church with his wife; McPhail was killed resisting arrest and the inquest found justifiable homicide.

framing.detail: The Statesman's headlines ('Sad End', 'An Unknown White Man Killed in a Bagino') center the killing at the brothel; the assault on 'a colored man' is reported as its cause without comment.
The Austin special in the Dallas and Waco dailies mentions the assault in one clause under 'A Pardoned Ex-Convict Killed by an Officer.'
The Savannah Morning News ran a one-sentence relay, 'An Ex-Horse Thief Killed', with no mention of Johnson.
